sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Interviewers use design pattern questions to assess whether you can write maintainable, extensible code — not just code that works once. Knowing SOLID principles and the six most common patterns gives you language to explain your design decisions and to recognise patterns you have already used without knowing their names.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **Creational** patterns (Singleton, Factory, Builder) handle object creation.
- **Structural** patterns (Decorator, Adapter, Proxy) handle how objects are composed.
- **Behavioural** patterns (Strategy, Observer, Command) handle how objects communicate.
- **SOLID** = five principles for writing classes that are easy to change.
- **Spring Boot** is pattern-heavy: beans are Singletons, ApplicationContext is a Factory, @Bean with @Builder is Builder, AOP is Decorator/Proxy, ApplicationEvents is Observer.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- SRP: one class, one reason to change. A UserService should not also send emails.
- OCP: add new features by adding new classes, not modifying existing ones.
- Singleton: Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default — you get this for free.
- Builder: Lombok @Builder generates it; know the problem it solves (telescoping constructors).
- Strategy: replace if/else chains with a family of interchangeable algorithm classes.
- Observer: event listener pattern — publisher/subscriber without tight coupling.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What is the Single Responsibility Principle?" → A class should have only one reason to change; separate concerns into separate classes.
- "How is Spring's bean scope related to the Singleton pattern?" → By default, Spring creates one instance of each bean and shares it — that is the Singleton pattern.
- "What problem does the Builder pattern solve?" → Telescoping constructor problem — too many constructor parameters; Builder makes object construction readable.
- "Give me a real-world example of the Strategy pattern." → Payment method selection (CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment implement PaymentStrategy interface).
- "What is the Observer pattern?" → An object (subject) maintains a list of dependents (observers) and notifies them of state changes; Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher is an example.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"I follow SOLID principles in my code. For example, I keep service classes focused — a UserService handles user operations, while a separate EmailService handles notifications. This follows SRP. In Spring Boot, I use the Strategy pattern when I have multiple payment methods — each implements a PaymentStrategy interface, and I can add new methods without changing existing code, which follows OCP. I use Lombok's @Builder for complex objects to avoid telescoping constructors."*
